title: Comparative Advantage
body: In 1817 David Ricardo showed that two countries gain from trade even if one is better at producing everything. What matters is the relative cost of what each gives up; his example was wine and cloth in Portugal and England.

title: The Invisible Hand
body: Adam Smith used the image in The Wealth of Nations in 1776. The idea is that individuals pursuing their own interest in a working market can promote the common good without intending to. The phrase appears only once in the book but became a symbol of market economics.

title: Keynesian Economics
body: In his General Theory (1936), John Maynard Keynes argued that an economy can get stuck with high unemployment when total demand is too weak. His conclusion, that governments can stabilise the economy through fiscal policy, shaped post-war policy.

title: The Wall Street Crash of 1929
body: Share prices on Wall Street collapsed in October 1929. The crash opened the Great Depression, the deepest economic crisis of the industrial era, which changed views on the role of the state in the economy.

title: The Bretton Woods System
body: At a 1944 conference the Allies agreed on fixed exchange rates tied to the US dollar, which was in turn convertible into gold. The IMF and the World Bank were founded there. The system broke down in the early 1970s after the US ended the dollar's convertibility into gold.

title: Tulip Mania
body: In the Netherlands in the 1630s, prices of tulip bulbs rose steeply and then collapsed in 1637. It is often cited as one of the first speculative bubbles, although historians now think its scale has been exaggerated.

title: The Oldest Central Bank
body: Sweden's Riksbank, founded in 1668, is the world's oldest central bank still in operation. It grew out of Stockholm's Banco, which had issued some of Europe's first banknotes.

title: Supply and Demand
body: The price of a good settles where the quantity buyers want equals the quantity sellers offer. Alfred Marshall compared supply and demand to the two blades of a pair of scissors: neither alone determines the price.

title: Opportunity Cost
body: The true cost of any choice is the value of the best alternative given up. An hour spent studying costs not only the time but whatever else that hour could have produced. The concept is central to economic reasoning.

title: The Quantity Theory of Money
body: The theory links the money supply to the price level: if money grows faster than the output of goods and services, prices tend to rise. Milton Friedman built on it to argue that inflation is ultimately a monetary phenomenon.

title: Compound Interest
body: With compound interest, interest is earned on previously earned interest, so growth accelerates over time. The 'rule of 72' gives a quick estimate: divide 72 by the annual percentage rate to get the number of years it takes for money to double.

title: Das Kapital
body: Karl Marx published the first volume of Das Kapital in 1867. He argued that profit comes from surplus value, the difference between what workers produce and what they are paid, and that capitalism contains the seeds of its own crisis. His ideas shaped 20th-century politics.

title: The 2008 Financial Crisis
body: Losses on US subprime mortgages spread through a global financial system loaded with debt and complex securities. The bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers in September 2008 triggered a panic and the deepest recession since the 1930s.

title: Gross Domestic Product
body: GDP measures the market value of all final goods and services produced in a country over a period. Simon Kuznets helped develop national accounts in the 1930s, and himself warned that GDP is not a measure of welfare.

title: Moral Hazard
body: Moral hazard arises when someone protected from the consequences of risk takes more risk. Insurance is the classic example; in finance, banks considered 'too big to fail' may take more risk if they expect to be rescued.

title: The Phillips Curve
body: In 1958 the New Zealand-born economist Bill Phillips found an inverse relationship between unemployment and the rate of wage increases in Britain over almost a century. Policymakers came to treat it as a menu: a little more inflation could buy lower unemployment. Milton Friedman and Edmund Phelps argued that the trade-off would vanish once people came to expect inflation, and the stagflation of the 1970s seemed to prove them right.

title: The Silver of Potosí
body: In 1545 the Spanish found an enormous silver deposit at Cerro Rico, a mountain in what is now Bolivia. Worked largely by indigenous labourers conscripted under the mita system, often in deadly conditions, Potosí grew into one of the largest cities of the Americas. Its silver flowed to Spain and onwards to Asia, financing Spanish power and Europe's trade with China.

title: The Market for Lemons
body: In 1970 George Akerlof showed how markets can break down when sellers know more than buyers. In a used-car market where buyers cannot tell good cars from bad 'lemons', they will pay only an average price, which drives owners of good cars away until mostly lemons remain. His work founded the economics of asymmetric information, which helps explain warranties, brands and compulsory insurance.

title: The Spice Trade
body: Pepper, cloves, nutmeg and cinnamon were among the most valuable goods in world trade for centuries, and cloves and nutmeg originally grew only on a few islands of the Moluccas in present-day Indonesia. The desire to reach these sources directly drove Portuguese, Spanish, Dutch and English voyages to Asia. Control of spice production became a goal of European colonial power, sometimes pursued with extreme violence.

title: India's 1991 Liberalisation
body: In 1991 India faced a balance-of-payments crisis, with foreign reserves enough for only a few weeks of imports. The government of Prime Minister Narasimha Rao, with Manmohan Singh as finance minister, devalued the rupee, cut tariffs and dismantled much of the 'Licence Raj' of industrial permits. The reforms marked India's turn from state-led planning towards a more open market economy and were followed by faster growth.

title: The Marginal Revolution
body: In the early 1870s William Stanley Jevons in England, Carl Menger in Austria and Léon Walras in Switzerland independently argued that value depends on marginal utility, the extra satisfaction from one more unit of a good. This resolved the old paradox of why water, essential to life, is cheap while diamonds are dear. Their work moved economics away from labour theories of value and laid the foundations of modern microeconomics.

title: The Lewis Dual-Sector Model
body: In 1954 the St Lucian economist Arthur Lewis described developing economies as having a traditional agricultural sector with surplus labour and a modern capitalist sector. As the modern sector grows, it can draw workers from agriculture without raising wages much, until the surplus is used up. Lewis shared the 1979 Nobel memorial prize in economics, becoming the first Black laureate in a category other than peace.

title: Price Elasticity of Demand
body: Price elasticity of demand measures how strongly the quantity bought responds to a change in price. Demand for necessities with few substitutes, such as fuel in the short run, is inelastic, so higher prices barely reduce purchases, while demand for goods with close substitutes is elastic. The concept, formalised by Alfred Marshall, helps explain why governments tax goods such as tobacco and how firms set prices.

title: Cacao Beans as Currency
body: In Mesoamerica, cacao beans served as a form of money alongside lengths of cotton cloth. In the Aztec world they were used for small purchases in great markets such as Tlatelolco and were also paid as tribute. Spanish accounts describe counterfeit beans made by filling empty husks with earth, and cacao continued to circulate as small change in parts of colonial Mexico.

title: Gresham's Law
body: Gresham's law states that 'bad money drives out good': when two coins have the same legal value but different metal content, people spend the debased coin and hoard the better one. It is named after the 16th-century English financier Sir Thomas Gresham, although Nicole Oresme and Nicolaus Copernicus had described the effect earlier. The name was given in the 19th century by the economist Henry Dunning Macleod.

title: Prospect Theory
body: The psychologists Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky proposed prospect theory in 1979 to describe how people actually make decisions under risk. People judge outcomes as gains or losses relative to a reference point, and losses loom larger than equivalent gains. Their work helped found behavioural economics, and Kahneman received the Nobel memorial prize in economics in 2002, after Tversky's death.

title: Debasement of the Roman Coinage
body: Roman emperors repeatedly reduced the silver content of the denarius and its successor coins to stretch limited bullion and pay their armies. During the crisis of the 3rd century AD the silver coinage was debased until it was little more than bronze with a thin silver wash. Prices rose sharply and trust in the currency collapsed, a classic case of inflation caused by debasing money.

title: Diminishing Returns
body: The law of diminishing returns states that adding more of one input, such as labour, to a fixed amount of another, such as land, eventually yields smaller and smaller increases in output. Classical economists including David Ricardo and Thomas Malthus used it to explain rising rents and the limits to food production. It underlies much economic reasoning about costs and production.

title: The Islamic Gold Dinar
body: In the 690s the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik replaced Byzantine- and Persian-style coins with a new gold dinar and silver dirham bearing Arabic religious inscriptions instead of images. The standardised coinage helped unify the economy of an empire stretching from North Africa to Central Asia. The dinar became one of the leading trade currencies of the medieval Mediterranean and Middle East.

title: The Malthusian Trap
body: In 1798 Thomas Malthus argued that population tends to grow geometrically while food supply grows only arithmetically. Any rise in living standards would therefore be absorbed by population growth until famine, disease or restraint brought it back down. His model fits much of pre-industrial history, but the sustained growth of productivity since the Industrial Revolution allowed much of the world to escape the trap.

title: The China Shock
body: After China joined the World Trade Organization in 2001, its exports of manufactured goods surged. The economists David Autor, David Dorn and Gordon Hanson found that the parts of the United States most exposed to Chinese import competition suffered lasting losses of manufacturing jobs and lower wages. Their research on this 'China shock' challenged the assumption that workers displaced by trade easily find other work.

title: The Drain of Wealth Theory
body: Dadabhai Naoroji, an Indian economist and politician, argued in the late 19th century that British rule was draining India's wealth. Through payments such as pensions and salaries of British officials and interest on debt, a large share of India's revenue flowed to Britain without return. His book Poverty and Un-British Rule in India (1901) shaped Indian nationalist economic thought.

title: The 1997 Asian Financial Crisis
body: In July 1997 Thailand was forced to abandon the peg of the baht to the US dollar after speculative attacks. Panic spread to Indonesia, South Korea, Malaysia and other economies that had borrowed heavily in foreign currencies, and their currencies and stock markets collapsed. The IMF's rescue packages, with conditions of austerity and reform, were highly controversial, and Indonesia's crisis contributed to the fall of Suharto in 1998.

title: The Arthashastra
body: The Arthashastra is an ancient Indian treatise on statecraft, economic policy and military strategy, traditionally attributed to Kautilya, adviser to the emperor Chandragupta Maurya. It discusses taxation, state control of mines and trade, market regulation and the management of the treasury. Many scholars think the surviving text was compiled and revised over several centuries, so its date and authorship are debated.

title: Inflation Targeting
body: In 1990 New Zealand became the first country to give its central bank an explicit inflation target, under the Reserve Bank of New Zealand Act of 1989. The bank was made independent in pursuing a low inflation range agreed with the government, and its governor was held accountable for meeting it. The approach spread to many central banks around the world, which commonly aim for inflation of about 2 per cent.

title: Indian Calicoes and the Calico Acts
body: In the 17th century, cheap and colourful cotton textiles from India, called calicoes after the port of Calicut, became highly fashionable in Europe. English wool and silk producers lobbied against them, and Parliament restricted them and then, in 1721, banned the use of most printed cotton cloth. Historians have argued that this protection, and the challenge of imitating Indian cloth, helped spur the mechanised British cotton industry.

title: The Resource Curse
body: Many studies have found that countries rich in oil or minerals often grow more slowly and are governed worse than resource-poor ones, a pattern called the resource curse. One mechanism is 'Dutch disease', named in 1977 after the Netherlands' experience following its natural gas discoveries: resource exports push up the currency and hurt other exports such as manufacturing. Volatile prices and corruption add to the problem, though countries such as Norway and Botswana show it can be avoided.

title: The Rochdale Pioneers
body: In 1844 a group of weavers and other workers in Rochdale, England, opened a cooperative shop selling flour, butter, sugar and oatmeal. Their Rochdale Principles, including open membership, one member one vote and the sharing of surplus among members according to their purchases, became the basis of the modern cooperative movement. Cooperatives built on these ideas spread worldwide in retail, farming, banking and housing.

title: Microfinance and the Grameen Bank
body: In 1976 the Bangladeshi economist Muhammad Yunus began lending small sums to poor villagers, mostly women, who had no access to banks. His Grameen Bank relied on groups of borrowers who supported one another, instead of on collateral. Yunus and the bank shared the 2006 Nobel Peace Prize, though later studies found microcredit's effect on poverty more modest than early supporters had hoped.

title: Public Goods
body: A public good is non-excludable, meaning no one can be prevented from using it, and non-rival, meaning one person's use does not reduce what is available to others. National defence, street lighting and basic research are standard examples. Because people can benefit without paying, markets tend to under-provide such goods, a free-rider problem that Paul Samuelson formalised in 1954 and that justifies much government spending.

title: The Solow Growth Model
body: In 1956 Robert Solow, and independently Trevor Swan in Australia, showed that adding capital alone cannot sustain growth, because each extra machine adds less output than the last. In their model, long-run growth in income per person comes from technological progress. Solow found that much of the growth in US output per worker could not be explained by more capital, a remainder known as the Solow residual.

title: The Discourses on Salt and Iron
body: In 81 BC the Han court of China held a debate over the state monopolies on salt and iron set up under Emperor Wu. Officials defended them as a source of revenue for defence, while Confucian scholars argued that the state should not compete with the people for profit. The record of the debate, the Discourses on Salt and Iron, is a classic early statement of the argument between state intervention and free enterprise.

title: The Gold Standard
body: Under the gold standard, a country's currency was convertible into a fixed amount of gold. Britain formalised it after the Napoleonic Wars, and in the 1870s many other major economies followed, creating fixed exchange rates that supported trade and investment. It tied governments' hands in recessions, however, and most countries abandoned it during the Great Depression of the 1930s.

title: Mercantilism
body: Mercantilism was the dominant economic outlook of European states from the 16th to the 18th centuries. It held that national wealth and power depended on accumulating gold and silver, so governments sought trade surpluses through tariffs, colonies and monopolies. Adam Smith attacked it in The Wealth of Nations, arguing that a nation's wealth lies in what it produces, not in its stock of precious metals.

title: The Waqf
body: A waqf is an endowment under Islamic law: property is dedicated in perpetuity, and its income supports a religious or charitable purpose. Waqfs funded mosques, schools, hospitals, fountains and caravanserais across the Islamic world, and at times held a large share of urban property. Some historians argue that the model influenced the development of charitable trusts in medieval Europe, though this is debated.

title: Bank Runs and Deposit Insurance
body: A bank run happens when depositors fear a bank will fail and rush to withdraw their money, which can bring down even a sound bank, since most deposits have been lent out. Waves of runs closed thousands of US banks in the early 1930s. In 1933 the United States created the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation to guarantee deposits, and runs on insured banks became rare.

title: Cowrie Shell Money
body: Cowrie shells, above all from the Maldives, served as money across large parts of Asia and Africa for centuries. Durable, hard to counterfeit and easy to count, they circulated as small change in Bengal and in West Africa, where they arrived through trans-Saharan and later European trade. Huge imports by European traders in the 18th and 19th centuries, including cheaper East African cowries from the 1840s, caused cowrie inflation, and colonial authorities eventually replaced them with coins.

title: The Physiocrats
body: The Physiocrats, a group of 18th-century French thinkers led by François Quesnay, are often regarded as the first school of economists. They held that only agriculture produced a net surplus, and Quesnay's Tableau économique (1758) traced how this surplus circulated between social classes. Their call for free trade in grain and a single tax on land influenced Adam Smith.

title: The Washington Consensus
body: The economist John Williamson coined the term in 1989 for ten policy reforms that Washington-based institutions such as the IMF, the World Bank and the US Treasury were urging on Latin American countries. They included fiscal discipline, trade liberalisation, privatisation and deregulation. The term came to stand for market-oriented reform in general, and critics blamed it for imposing austerity on developing countries as a condition of loans.

title: Diocletian's Edict on Maximum Prices
body: In 301 AD the Roman emperor Diocletian issued an edict fixing maximum prices for hundreds of goods and services, from grain to wages, on pain of death. It was meant to curb the inflation that had followed the debasement of the coinage. According to the Christian writer Lactantius, goods vanished from the markets, and the edict was soon ignored, making it a classic early example of the failure of price controls.

title: Bitcoin
body: In 2008 a person or group using the name Satoshi Nakamoto published a design for Bitcoin, a digital currency that works without a central bank or other trusted intermediary. Transactions are recorded on a public ledger, the blockchain, maintained by a decentralised network of computers. Bitcoin launched in 2009 and inspired thousands of other cryptocurrencies, though economists debate whether such volatile assets can serve well as money.

title: Limited Liability
body: Under limited liability, shareholders can lose only what they invested in a company, not their personal assets. Britain made it widely available to ordinary companies through laws passed in 1855 and 1856, and other industrial countries adopted similar rules. By making it safer for many small investors to buy shares, it allowed the large-scale raising of capital that built railways and industrial corporations.

title: Economies of Scale
body: Economies of scale arise when the average cost of each unit falls as output grows, for example because fixed costs are spread over more units or larger plants allow more specialisation. They help explain why industries such as car manufacturing and power generation tend to be dominated by large firms. Where they are very strong, a single firm can supply a market most cheaply, creating a 'natural monopoly' that governments often regulate.
